faqs.question: How do Spanish speakers say "chat someone up"?
faqs.answer: The everyday verb is ligar, and coquetear is the neutral word for flirting. In Mexico you will also hear echarle los perros, which El Colegio de México's dictionary marks as popular usage for making your interest in someone obvious.

faqs.question: What does "de miedo" mean in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Literally "of fear", but the Real Academia Española lists it as a colloquial phrase used to praise something. So "te queda de miedo" can mean a costume looks great on you, a double meaning English cannot copy.

faqs.question: How do you say trick or treat in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Most of Latin America says dulce o truco. Spain usually says truco o trato, and because trato also means a deal, it gives you an extra pun.

faqs.question: Is Day of the Dead the same as Halloween?
faqs.answer: No, though they are cousins. Mexico's INAH traces the 1 and 2 November feasts to medieval Europe's All Saints' and All Souls' days, with All Saints' fixed on 1 November around 835 beside the Celtic Samhain of 31 October. Keep flirty lines for 31 October and any Day of the Dead line gentle.

faqs.question: Are piropos illegal in Spain?
faqs.answer: A friendly compliment to someone already talking to you is not. Since Ley Orgánica 10/2022, article 173.4 of the Penal Code covers sexual remarks that create an objectively humiliating, hostile or intimidating situation, punishable by 5 to 30 days of home confinement or community service on the victim's complaint.

faqs.question: How do you pronounce calabaza?
faqs.answer: Say kah-lah-BAH-sah in Latin America and the US, where the z sounds like an s. In most of Spain the z is a soft th, so it becomes kah-lah-BAH-thah.

faqs.question: Should I use tú or usted when flirting in Spanish?
faqs.answer: Use tú. Usted is the polite, distant form you would use with a stranger's grandmother, so it cancels the flirting before the pun lands.

faqs.question: Can I write my Halloween page in Spanish?
faqs.answer: The parts you type are yours, including the letter, the pumpkin word and the closing question, which is editable up to 60 characters. The page's own buttons and steps are in English, so a partner who reads no English may prefer a handwritten card.

faqs.question: What is a cute Spanish Halloween nickname for a partner?
faqs.answer: Calabacita, little pumpkin, is the safest, with the bonus joke that in Mexico it also means a courgette. Mi boo works in Spanglish, and brujita, little witch, is affectionate if they like the costume.

faqs.question: Do Spanish pickup lines work better by text?
faqs.answer: For someone whose number you already have, usually yes, because they read it when they like. Across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page averages 11.1 views, so a written line gets reread.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Pickup Lines in Spanish: 35 Piropos With Glosses

The Halloween pickup lines in Spanish that land are the ones that only work in Spanish: puns on *calabaza* (pumpkin), *de miedo* (scary, and colloquially "amazing") and *dulce* (sweet, and candy). Send them to someone who already knows you; never shout them at a stranger. A written line also gets reread: across SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone and each page averages 11.1 views.

Below are 35 original, clean lines with glosses and pronunciation hints. After them come regional flirting words, Día de los Muertos and where a piropo becomes harassment.

## What is a piropo, and is it a pickup line?

A piropo is a short compliment about someone's qualities, usually their looks. The Real Academia Española [defines piropo](https://dle.rae.es/piropo) as a "dicho breve" praising someone, "especially the beauty of a woman".

A piropo can open a conversation, or be tossed at a passer-by who never asked. In a 2023 paper in ITAM's journal *Isonomía*, [Anna Richter weighs three attitudes to piropos](https://isonomia.itam.mx/index.php/revista-cientifica/article/view/672), positive, neutral and negative, argues for the negative one, and proposes a test that still lets people approach each other (abstract read only).

## 29 Halloween pickup lines in Spanish, by word

Every line uses informal *tú*, never *usted*. Where a word ends in o/a, pick your ending.

### 1. Calabaza lines: pumpkins and other halves

These lines play on the pumpkin itself, the one object every Halloween doorstep shares. Say kah-lah-BAH-sah in Latin America, kah-lah-BAH-thah in most of Spain.

- "Contigo hasta la calabaza más fea parece obra de arte." ("With you around, even the ugliest pumpkin looks like art.")
- "¿Me ayudas a escoger calabaza? Prometo no tardar más de tres horas." ("Help me pick a pumpkin? I promise it won't take more than three hours.")
- "Eres mi media calabaza." ("You're my other half," twisting *media naranja*, Spanish for soulmate.)
- "Te digo calabacita de cariño, no porque seas verde." ("I call you little pumpkin out of love, not because you're green." In Mexico *calabacita*, kah-lah-bah-SEE-tah, is also a courgette.)

### 2. Fantasma lines: ghosts and ghosting

Say fahn-TAHS-mah. The RAE also lists it for a vain show-off.

- "No me hagas ghosting: el fantasma aquí soy yo." ("Don't ghost me. I'm the ghost here.")
- "Vine de fantasma para pasar desapercibido, y me viste igual." ("I came as a ghost to go unnoticed, and you spotted me anyway.")
- "Ojo: un fantasma también es un fanfarrón. Yo solo soy quien lleva la sábana." ("Careful: a fantasma is also a show-off. I'm just the one in the sheet.")
- "Me quedé en blanco, y no por el disfraz." ("My mind went blank, and not because of the costume." *Quedarse en blanco* is literally "to go white".)

### 3. Bruja and hechizo lines

Say *bruja* (witch) as BROO-hah. *Hechizo* (spell) is eh-CHEE-soh, or eh-CHEE-thoh in Spain.

- "¿Qué hechizo usaste? No me sale ni una frase." ("What spell did you use? I can't get a sentence out.")
- "Tengo escoba, pero contigo prefiero ir caminando." ("I've got a broom, but with you I'd rather walk.")
- "¿Me das un aventón en tu escoba?" ("Can I get a lift on your broom?" *Aventón* is Mexican for a ride.)
- "No creo en brujas, pero tú me tienes embrujado." ("I don't believe in witches, but you've bewitched me," riffing on the proverb *yo no creo en las brujas, pero que las hay, las hay*.)
- "Rompe el hechizo y dime cómo te llamas." ("Break the spell and tell me your name.")

### 4. Susto and miedo lines

*Susto* (SOOS-toh) is a fright. The RAE lists *de miedo* colloquially as plain praise.

- "Ese disfraz te queda de miedo, y lo digo en los dos sentidos." ("That costume looks scary on you, and I mean both senses.")
- "Qué susto: casi me voy sin hablarte." ("What a fright: I nearly left without talking to you.")
- "Estoy muerto de ganas de invitarte a un café." ("I'm dying to buy you a coffee.")
- "Me das miedo, de lo nervioso que me pones." ("You scare me, that's how nervous you make me.")

### 5. Dulce o truco lines

Most of Latin America says *dulce o truco* (DOOL-seh oh TROO-koh). Spain usually says *truco o trato*, and *trato* also means "a deal".

- "¿Dulce o truco? Sin truco: solo quería saber tu nombre." ("Trick or treat? No trick: I just wanted your name.")
- "Eres más dulce que toda mi bolsa de dulces." ("You're sweeter than my whole bag of candy.")
- "Truco o trato: el trato es un café, el truco es que invito yo." ("The deal is a coffee; the trick is that I'm paying.")
- "Vine por dulces y me voy con un crush." ("I came for candy and I'm leaving with a crush.")

### 6. Calavera, momia and vampiro lines

- "Te quiero hasta los huesos." ("I love you down to the bones.")
- "¿Eres momia? Porque me tienes envuelto." ("Are you a mummy? You've got me wrapped up.")
- "No muerdo, pero los tacos sí los invito." ("I don't bite, but the tacos are on me.")

### 7. Spanglish lines for texting someone you know

- "Happy Halloween, mi calabacita."
- "This costume needs a pareja. ¿Te apuntas?" ("...needs a partner. Are you in?")
- "Mi plan para el 31: tú, una peli de miedo y cero sustos de verdad." ("My plan for the 31st: you, a horror film, zero real frights.")
- "I'm not scared of ghosts, pero sí de que me digas que no." ("...but I am scared you'll say no.")
- "No necesito disfraz para que me reconozcas: soy quien te escribe cada día." ("No costume needed: I'm the one who texts you every day.")

## 6 Día de los Muertos lines that stay respectful

Día de los Muertos is not Mexican Halloween, though the two are cousins. An [essay by INAH archaeologist Víctor Joel Santos Ramírez](https://inah.gob.mx/especiales-inah/articulos/el-origen-del-dia-de-muertos) traces the 1 and 2 November feasts to medieval Europe's All Saints' and All Souls' days, with Pope Gregory IV fixing All Saints' on 1 November around 835, beside the Celtic Samhain of 31 October; older Mesoamerican funerary beliefs survived inside them.

Keep these for someone who celebrates it. Wait until they have invited you in.

- "Eres como el camino de cempasúchil: me llevas a casa." ("Like a path of marigolds, you lead me home." Say sem-pah-SOO-cheel.)
- "¿Compartimos un pan de muerto? Yo pongo el chocolate." ("Share a pan de muerto? I'll bring the hot chocolate.")
- "Te escribiría una calaverita, pero solo me salen versos de amor." ("I'd write you a calaverita, the day's joking verse, but only love poems come out.")
- "Quiero conocer tu ofrenda y a quién recuerdas en ella." ("I'd love to see your ofrenda and hear who you remember on it.")
- "¿Me acompañas a ver las ofrendas del centro? Prometo escuchar más que hablar." ("Show me the altars in town? I'll listen more than I talk.")
- "Me gustas más que el pan de muerto, y eso es decir mucho." ("I like you more than pan de muerto, and that's saying something.")

## Piropo, ligar or echar los perros: which word where

*Coquetear* (to flirt) is neutral everywhere, and *ligar* is the everyday verb for chatting someone up. For Mexico, El Colegio de México's dictionary lists [*echarle los perros a alguien*](https://dem.colmex.mx/Ver/perro), marked popular, as making your interest obvious. *Tirarle los perros*, often taught to learners, is not listed.

*Piropo* is the same word everywhere. What differs is who hears it.

## Street piropos vs flirting with someone you know

The line is consent, and Spain wrote it into law: [Ley Orgánica 10/2022 of 6 September](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-14630) rewrote article 173.4 of the Penal Code to cover sexual "expressions, behaviour or propositions" that create an objectively humiliating, hostile or intimidating situation. The penalty is 5 to 30 days of home confinement or community service, prosecuted only on the victim's complaint.

A 2019 paper by [Fernanda Chacon Onetto in *Revista Estudos Feministas*](https://www.scielo.br/j/ref/a/DdjM6fbwmmwZSFmBmNBM5wQ/?lang=es) summarises surveys in which 76% of Chilean respondents reported street harassment within 12 months, and 93% of 1,300 Argentine women did. The table runs from the worst place for a line to the best.

| Where the line goes | Time it takes | Consent | Measured result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shouted at a stranger | 3 seconds | None; Spain's art. 173.4 can apply | Don't |
| At a party, to someone talking to you | 3 seconds | They chose the conversation | Not measured |
| Texted to someone whose number you have | Under 1 minute | They gave you the number | Not measured |
| Halloween greeting page for a partner | About 5 minutes | Private link, opened when they like | 48.3% opened on a phone; 11.1 views per page |
| Premium Halloween page | About 10 minutes | Private link, one reply up to 280 characters | 90.9% of started pages published |

Same words, different person, different act. Only two rows involve a page.

## Sending a Spanish line to your partner on 31 October

If they are already yours, a line can become the question. The [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes a letter, up to six photos and the word to carve on the pumpkin; the closing question, "Will you be my boo?" by default, is editable up to 60 characters, so "¿Quieres ser mi boo?" fits easily.

They knock three times and carve the jack-o'-lantern until your word glows. You get an email the first time they answer.

One limit: the interface is English, so your Spanish sits inside English buttons. To let them hear your accent, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note up to 60 seconds.

## When a Spanish pickup line is the wrong move

Skip it with a stranger in the street. Skip the Día de los Muertos lines with anyone grieving this year; on 1 and 2 November a hand to hold beats a pun.

With a native speaker you barely know, a learner's piropo can read as a party trick; Spanglish admits you are trying. SubhSandesh loses too: a partner who reads no English will meet English buttons, so a handwritten card works better.

- Richter, A., *Isonomía* 58, 10 June 2023 (abstract only).
- Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH), "El origen del Día de Muertos" (undated).

auditReport.honestAssessment: No page in the US top 10 actually gives Halloween lines in Spanish. The results are general Spanish pickup-line lists (LingQ, Spanish Academy), English Halloween lists (Cosmopolitan, Reader's Digest), kids' jokes and social posts. An answer engine has checkable reasons to cite this post: Spanish-only wordplay glossed and pronounced, a sourced Día de los Muertos distinction, and Spain's art. 173.4 penalty. After remediation the strongest pun, dar calabazas, is gone because no fetched dictionary verified it, so the calabaza section is now ordinary pumpkin lines any translated list could match. The many unsourced regional glosses (aventón, calabacita, media naranja) rest on the writer's Spanish. The first-party numbers are platform-wide, not Spanish- or Halloween-specific, and the INAH source still fails the swap test. Lingq.com and cosmopolitan.com have far more domain authority, so a ranking will take months, not weeks.
